title: Span<T>, Memory<T> and ref structs
description: Master Span<T> and Memory<T> for zero-allocation slicing, understand ref struct restrictions, and apply these types in performance-critical code.

data.text: `Span<T>` and `Memory<T>` are the foundation of modern high-performance .NET code. They represent a contiguous region of memory — an array slice, a string segment, a stack-allocated buffer — without allocating a new object. Before `Span<T>` existed, slicing an array required `ArraySegment<T>`, which created a wrapper object and did not work with strings or stack memory. `Span<T>` unifies all these scenarios into a single, allocation-free abstraction that the JIT can optimize aggressively.

The key difference between `Span<T>` and `Memory<T>` is their lifetime restrictions. `Span<T>` is a `ref struct` — it can only live on the stack. You cannot store a `Span<T>` in a class field, a `Dictionary`, or an async method's state machine. `Memory<T>` is a regular `struct` that can be stored anywhere, including heap-allocated objects. `Memory<T>` provides a `Span` property when you need to access the underlying memory. This design gives you both safety (the compiler prevents dangling references) and flexibility (async methods can use `Memory<T>`).

`Span<T>` is a `ref struct` backed by a pointer and a length. The pointer can point to a managed array, a stack-allocated buffer from `stackalloc`, or memory on the stack obtained via `MemoryMarshal`. Because `Span<T>` lives on the stack, the GC can never move it while it is in scope — the compiler guarantees that `Span<T>` never escapes the method that created it. This makes `Span<T>` safe to use with pointers and unmanaged code.

data.title: Span<T> slicing without allocation

data.text: `stackalloc` allocates memory directly on the current thread's stack. In safe code, the allocated memory is automatically bounded — you cannot allocate more than a few kilobytes, and the runtime tracks the bounds. The result is a `Span<T>` that points to the stack buffer. When the method returns, the stack frame is destroyed and the memory is reclaimed. No heap allocation, no GC pressure, no cleanup needed.

data.title: Using stackalloc for a small buffer

data.text: `Memory<T>` wraps the same underlying memory as `Span<T>` but without the stack-only restriction. You can store `Memory<T>` in a class field, pass it to async methods, and keep it for as long as you need. When you are ready to access the data, call `.Span` to get a `Span<T>` view. This indirection is the key to using sliceable memory in async code.

data.title: Using Memory<T> in an async method

data.text: ref struct restrictions: what Span<T> cannot do

Because `Span<T>` is a `ref struct`, the C# compiler enforces strict rules. You cannot box a `Span<T>`, store it in a `Dictionary`, use it as a generic type argument without constraints, or capture it in a lambda. You cannot `await` inside a method that contains a `Span<T>` local variable. These restrictions exist because the compiler cannot prove that a `Span<T>` would not outlive the stack frame it was created in. The rules are strict, but they prevent an entire class of memory-safety bugs.

data.title: Cannot await in a method that holds a Span<T>
data.text: If your method allocates a `Span<T>` and then hits an `await`, the compiler will reject it. The span lives on the stack, but `await` splits the method into a state machine that may resume on a different stack frame. To work around this, use `Memory<T>` instead, or process the span synchronously before awaiting. This is the single most common `ref struct` restriction developers encounter.

data.caption: Span<T> and Memory<T> provide zero-allocation views into memory from arrays, strings, and stackalloc buffers.

data.title: Key takeaways
items: `Span<T>` is a stack-only, allocation-free view over contiguous memory from arrays, strings, or stackalloc.
`Memory<T>` is the heap-safe alternative that can be stored in fields and passed to async methods.
`ref struct` restrictions prevent `Span<T>` from being boxed, stored in collections, or captured across await points.
`stackalloc` allocates on the thread stack and is automatically reclaimed when the method returns.
